I've been an avid fan of Stephen King since my teens ... his brand of supernatural evil is scary (pun intended!)

However I must say I've been disappointed in the last couple of books published. Mr. Mercedes and now Finders Keepers (I'm about 3/4 of the way through) - although good stories about very evil people ... nothing supernatural, sci-fi or in this day and age even unbelievable.

I'm really hoping he hasn't run out of ideas! What do you think?

The guy had a very hard time of things after being hit by that van back in 1999. Accidents like that can be life changing. He is more reflect and it shows. He still has ideas, but his writing style mirrors the changes in his life and perceptions. Besides, the man has published 54 books and nearly 200 short stories. If you have ever read any of the Bachman books, then we can probably agree not all of them are classics. If you truly love his work, keep reading. He may come back to the intensity that first attracted you. Or, you may learn to appreciate the richer characters, deeper relationships and more complex stories of his recent work.

Good points - I have read all the Bachman books albeit a couple of decades ago :) There were some very good ones mixed with as you say non-classics...

I certainly am not giving up and will read anything written by the man as I find everything he writes enjoyable ..just hoping he goes back to what made him an American legend

I know this is an old comment but v/books needs more love and I totally agree with your point. I had the same idea myself.

Personally I classify King's work in 3 main eras:

  1. When he first started getting published
  2. After he got clean from drugs and alcohol
  3. After the van accident

Each era has its own style, and each has good books and bad books.
It's crazy how much Doctor Sleep is about "After he got clean from drugs and alcohol".
AFAIK he does have a staff of ghost writers..

Can you cite a source for that claim?

I know for a fact that James Patterson has a staff of ghost writers, but I've never once heard that King employs them. In fact, in an interview with Patterson he poked fun at King for being angry at Patterson's success because Patterson had been aided by ghost writers.

King does produce a high volume of work, but that's because - according to On Writing, his memoir, he writes at least 2000 words every single day, including on his birthday and Christmas.
I read it in a magazine awhile back, but doing a google search came up with this? http://ha.ckerne.ws/2013/04/01/exclusive-stephen-king-hacked/

I find that suspicious, mostly because it was posted on April 1st, 2013. And it also references that they were working on Christine 2 (according to the article, they were beginning this work around March 30th, 2013), which does not exist. Seeing as it's been more than 2 years, I would expect that project to be done.

So, long story short, that article is blatantly fake. Look more closely at your sources next time.

I doubt I'm as much as a fan as you (I've only read a half dozen of his books) but I think he's always sort of moved between supernatural and "profane". Wow Rage ... one of the Bachman books ... It has been forever I read that one. If I remember correctly - you're right - nothing supernatural in that one specifically, but as it was a short story combined with others that were - I didn't count it.

Misery - another good example of pure evil ... a good story. Much better than that movie made it look!

The Green Mile - the John Coffey could cure/eat illness/death ... supernatural twist

Hearts in Atlantis - another grouping of short stories ... the Low Men and the tie into the Crimson King in the Dark Tower series made it an interesting set for me.

You've read the Stand and that is by far my favorite ... I go back and re-read every few years ... a great story every time!

Some of his others you might want to try are The Dark Tower series, IT and the Tommyknockers
I absolutely love the Stand, it started my love of reading. I should go back and reread it!

If you haven't already, read the uncut version of The Stand. It adds something insane like 200-250 pages of cut story lines. I had only read the uncut version and then read the final cut and couldn't belive some of the story they cut, especially Trashman.

King's style has always been kind of all over the place. Ever read Eyes of the Dragon? It's mid-evil fantasy. King is best known for his horror, but he isn't limited at all to it. He's a wicked pissah.

I feel like that too. I love all of Kings work, but I will always have a special spot in my heart for the books he wrote when he was crazy off of drugs and depression. I'm glad he is better now, and especially glad he recovered from his car accident, but his books have become a lot more tame since then.

If you want to see just how much his writing style changes, read the Dark Tower books. Since they are a series he wrote over a course of decades they are a really excellent way to see his progression.

My dad handed me Salem's Lot, my 1st king book back in the dark ages (late 70's) when I was just a kid. My 1st paper in middle school (6th grade) was written about him. This hurts me a lot to say: Although it is hard to track which stories he started before his sobriety in 1986ish, this seems to be the beginning of his decline. No Junk no soul. :( That being said, I applaud his sobriety. I would much rather have him around and writing than dead at the bottom of a bottle. We have all been lucky to keep him around. There are still gems buried in his later work and his endings in them have improved. I'm not a big fan of the Dark Tower, having been spoiled at an early age by such masterpieces as Night Shift, The Shining, etc, etc, etc. but I recognize it as a great work. I still read his newer stuff and have hope each time that they will be a golden work.
Salem's Lot was my first King read as well - also around the same age ... I remember sleeping with a cross for at least 6 months afterwards!!!
Yeah it's terrible to say, but it does seem like without coke fueling him, he seems to be much more demure.

Doctor Sleep, which released in 2013, was plenty supernatural. Revival - which came out just 8 or so months ago - was also supernatural.

Meanwhile, King's 1999 novel Hearts in Atlantis was a straight drama with no horror/supernatural aspects. (Edit: After thinking about it, that isn't entirely right, but it's still less supernatural than many of his works...)

King is a very flexible author who doesn't necessarily care about genre. He tends to write whatever he wants, whenever he wants. You're referencing two books from a trilogy that he's currently working through, and it makes sense that two books from the same trilogy would be consistent (either both supernatural or both not).
I didn't know it was a trilogy - thanks for the update! Makes sense now the sideline in the 2nd book about Brady ...

I don't think he's run out of ideas, I think he's just taking a break from his normal routine. This isn't even the first time he's done something like this - the Richard Bachman books were pretty different from his normal style. When you get to be at King's level of success, you have some room to wiggle your toes and try something else out for a while. Plus, I thought 11/22/63 was pretty much his best standalone work, and that wasn't anything like what he normally writes.
While I agree that he's been hit and miss in the 2000s, Duma Key and 11/12/63 are two of his best novels IMO.

I agree completely.

Duma Key is one of the best novels I've ever read. I would love to read another one like that, even if it isn't by King.

11/12/63 is also very good. A smart time travel novel that focused on the time period and the impression of it. Also would love to read a similar book.

I haven't read the last couple, but I think he's gotten more contemplative with maturity. He has to go with what interests him, and churning out similar pieces of work was bound to get old eventually.

He's gotten older and more retrospective. I think he had always wanted to write noir and period novels but had never gotten around to doing it and had put it off in favor of his horror and Tower stuff. Growing older may have given him the nudge to move in this direction and maybe his experience in writing 11/22/63 was a segway into this new direction.

Honestly I'm satisfied that the Tower novels were finished and then we even got dessert with Wind Through the Keyhole.
I have to say I feel the same way but I am hoping that he's going to have a comeback!
